answer.rationale:
The two symptoms this quarter are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and the inherited record points at onboarding friction as the mechanism most directly upstream of both (memory_86 on shortened onboarding, memory_31 on field reduction at signup, memory_91 on in-product activation nudges as the downstream complement). Simplifying onboarding attacks the causal root rather than the symptom, and it does not spend price integrity to do it, so it is the option most consistent with sustainable long-term qualified revenue.

I am spending verification on memory_73 first because it is the memory most likely to pull the org toward the wrong move. The competitor's entry pricing makes a 40% discount emotionally obvious, and memory_73 appears to bless it with a 31% activation and 18% revenue gain. That pairing is internally strange: a 40% price cut needs roughly a 67% volume increase just to hold revenue flat, so an 18% revenue gain on a 31% activation lift does not reconcile unless something else moved (mix shift, an annual-prepay term, a concurrent page change, or revenue measured as bookings rather than realized). The note that the pricing page 'was not otherwise altered' reads like a summarizer's reassurance rather than a recorded control. I want the original record to see the denominator and whether the lift was incremental or pulled-forward demand. If it holds up it becomes a real option; if it is confounded, acting on it would train customers to wait for discounts and permanently degrade the SMB price anchor — the value-eroding failure mode here.

Second pull is memory_86, because it is the load-bearing memory for my intended action and it is a day-52 consolidation that may simply be a restatement of memory_31 (day 12) rather than independent evidence. If those two are the same study reported twice, my apparent evidence base is half as thick as it looks and I should size accordingly.

I am not treating referral_incentive or enterprise_sales_assist as this week's move: neither addresses the observed funnel decay, and memory_57's 'no measurable harm to retention' is an absence-of-evidence claim, not evidence of absence. Standard experiment scale with a held-out control and instrumentation on activation quality, not just activation count — a lift that arrives as unqualified accounts is not the objective. Holding this as a working hypothesis, not a settled finding, pending what the archive returns.
